Action Plan:
1. Arrange emergency ambulance transport to nearest stroke-capable Emergency Department for suspected acute cerebrovascular event; doctor remained on the line until crew arrival.  
2. Advise patient to unlock front door and sit in hallway to facilitate paramedic access.  
3. Hospital team to perform urgent neuro-imaging (CT/CTA brain) and stroke assessment for possible reperfusion therapy (thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy) once exact onset window clarified.  
4. Provide hand-off to ambulance dispatch with clinical details and vascular risk factors (HTN, T2DM).  
5. Counsel patient regarding stroke warning signs and need for immediate hospital care; patient verbalised understanding.  
6. Document chronic disease history (hypertension, type 2 diabetes) for in-hospital medication reconciliation and secondary-prevention planning.  
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden inability to move left arm noticed on awakening ~1 hour before call.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Tingling on left side of face since onset.  
  – Mild dysphagia (spilled drink).  
  – Speech feels slower/more difficult (dysarthria).  
  – No pain, no left-leg symptoms, no facial droop seen by patient, no headache or loss of consciousness.  
• Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension.  
• Medications: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented); Losartan (dose/route/frequency not documented); Amlodipine (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Allergies: Penicillin.  
• Family history: Father with “heart disease” (details unspecified).  
• Social history: Lives alone; former smoker; drinks several pints of beer on weekends and a couple during the week.

Objective:
• Telephone consultation—no direct physical examination possible.  
• Patient reports:  
  – Persistent inability to move left arm.  
  – Left arm painless, warm, no discoloration.  
  – No subjective facial asymmetry observed, but facial tingling present.  
  – Speech noted by patient and clinician to be slower.  
• Vitals: not obtained remotely.  
• No laboratory or imaging results available yet.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Sudden left arm paralysis with facial tingling and dysarthria  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke (DDx item: “Acute ischemic stroke” – High).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Intracerebral hemorrhage (DDx – Medium): Hypertensive risk; needs CT to exclude.  
     • Transient ischemic attack (DDx – Medium): Deficits ongoing; less likely but cannot be excluded until resolution observed.  
     • Other causes (e.g., peripheral nerve compression, hypoglycemia) considered low likelihood per DDx; facial and speech symptoms make them less probable.  
   - Investigations planned: Emergent CT brain ± CTA/MRI per hospital stroke protocol; point-of-care glucose on arrival; full stroke blood panel.  
   - Treatment planned: Expedite to ED for potential IV thrombolysis/thrombectomy; supportive care en route; hospital to commence antiplatelet/anticoagulation or antihypertensive management per findings.  
   - Relevant referrals: Immediate ED/stroke team activation via ambulance service.

2. Hypertension  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Chronic essential hypertension (known).  
   - Differential diagnosis: n/a (chronic, already diagnosed).  
   - Investigations planned: Hospital to review BP control; consider inpatient adjustment.  
   - Treatment planned: Continue current agents (Losartan, Amlodipine) unless contraindicated during acute stroke management; future secondary-prevention optimisation.  
   - Relevant referrals: Primary care follow-up post-discharge for BP monitoring.

3. Type 2 diabetes mellitus  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (established).  
   - Differential diagnosis: n/a.  
   - Investigations planned: Hospital to check capillary and serum glucose; HbA1c for long-term control.  
   - Treatment planned: Continue Metformin unless contraindicated (e.g., renal impairment); consider escalation if control suboptimal post-event.  
   - Relevant referrals: Diabetes nurse educator/endocrinology as needed for secondary prevention of cerebrovascular disease.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: Objective vitals, formal neurological examination, blood glucose level, medication dosages, vaccination status.  
• Internal conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio; brief pauses but clinically adequate.
